name: Java
description: The JVM memory model, collections, generics erasure, equals/hashCode and the concurrency toolkit.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Java is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is Java, and what is it mainly used for?
cards.answer: A general-purpose, statically typed, object-oriented language that runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). It is a mainstay of large enterprise back ends, financial systems and big-data tooling, and was the original language for Android apps.
cards.explanation: Java's strengths are stability, tooling and backwards compatibility: code written decades ago still runs. Frameworks such as Spring Boot power a large share of corporate web services, and the JVM also hosts other languages (Kotlin, Scala, Clojure).

cards.prompt: Who created Java, and what was its famous promise?
cards.answer: James Gosling and his team at Sun Microsystems, released in 1995. The promise was "write once, run anywhere": compile once to bytecode and run it on any machine that has a JVM.
cards.explanation: Oracle acquired Sun in 2010 and now stewards Java, which is developed in the open as OpenJDK. A new feature release ships every six months, with a long-term-support (LTS) release every two years.

cards.prompt: How does Java code get from a `.java` file to a running program?
cards.answer: `javac` compiles source into platform-independent bytecode (`.class` files); the JVM then runs that bytecode, interpreting it at first and JIT-compiling hot methods to native machine code.
cards.explanation: The bytecode layer is what makes Java portable across operating systems and CPUs. It also means a Java program needs a JVM installed (or bundled) to run. For quick experiments, `java Hello.java` compiles and runs a single file in one step.

cards.prompt: What does the classic minimal Java program look like?
cards.answer: A class with a `public static void main(String[] args)` method — the entry point the JVM calls. `System.out.println` prints a line.
cards.explanation: Everything in Java lives inside a class, which is why even "hello world" needs one. Modern Java (JDK 25) also allows a much shorter "compact source file" with a bare `void main()`, aimed at beginners and scripts, but the classic form is what you will read in most existing code.

cards.prompt: What kind of language is Java: typing, memory and paradigms?
cards.answer: Statically and strongly typed: every variable has a declared (or inferred, with `var`) type checked at compile time. Memory is garbage collected — you allocate with `new` and never free. It is class-based object-oriented, with functional features (lambdas, streams) added since Java 8.
cards.explanation: Static typing makes Java verbose compared with Python, but it lets the compiler and IDE catch errors and refactor huge codebases safely. Garbage collection removes whole classes of memory bugs at the cost of some run-time overhead.

cards.prompt: What are Maven and Gradle?
cards.answer: Java's two main build tools. They compile code, run tests, package JARs and download dependencies from repositories such as Maven Central. Maven uses an XML `pom.xml`; Gradle uses a Groovy or Kotlin build script.
cards.explanation: Both use the same dependency coordinates (`group:artifact:version`) and the same central repository, so a library is equally available to either. Gradle is the default for Android; Maven remains common in enterprise back ends.

modules.name: Language & Object Contracts
modules.description: References, equality, immutability and the contracts every Java object must honour.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer: hello world | hello
cards.explanation: Java is always pass-by-value — the *reference* is copied. Mutating the object through the copied reference is visible to the caller; reassigning the parameter is not. `String` is immutable, so `s + " world"` creates a new object the caller never sees.

resources.title: Oracle — Passing information to a method

cards.prompt: What is the equals/hashCode contract, and what breaks when you violate it?
cards.answer: Equal objects must return equal hash codes; hashCode must be stable while the object is in a hash-based collection. Break it and `HashMap`/`HashSet` lookups silently fail to find objects that are equal.
cards.explanation: A HashMap finds the bucket by hashCode, then compares with equals. Overriding one without the other, or mutating a field used in hashCode after insertion, strands the entry in a bucket nobody will look in again. Use immutable keys.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer: true false true
cards.explanation: String literals are interned in a shared pool, so `a` and `b` are the same object. `new String(...)` forces a fresh object on the heap. This is the canonical demonstration of why you compare strings with `equals`, never `==`.

cards.prompt: Checked vs unchecked exceptions
cards.answer: Checked extend `Exception` and must be declared or handled; unchecked extend `RuntimeException` (or `Error`) and need neither.

left.title: Checked
points: Pollutes signatures up the call stack

right.title: Unchecked
points: Can escape silently to the top

cards.explanation: Modern practice leans on unchecked exceptions plus explicit result types, because checked exceptions force every intermediate layer to either handle or re-declare — which in practice produces empty catch blocks.

cards.prompt: Why will this not compile, and what does it tell you about Java generics?
cards.answer: Generics are erased at compile time — there is no `T` at runtime to test against. Pass a `Class<T>` and use `clazz.isInstance(o)` instead.
cards.explanation: Erasure means no `new T[]`, no `T.class`, and no overloads that differ only in type parameters. The compiler inserts casts for you; at runtime a `List<String>` is just a `List`. This is the price paid for backwards compatibility with pre-generics bytecode.

cards.prompt: What does a `record` give you?
cards.answer: An immutable, final data carrier with a canonical constructor, accessors, and generated `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` derived from its components.
cards.explanation: Records remove the boilerplate that made value objects painful, and they work with pattern matching and sealed interfaces to give Java algebraic-data-type ergonomics. Components are shallowly immutable — a record holding a mutable list is still mutable through that list.

modules.name: JVM, Collections & Concurrency
modules.description: Garbage collection, collection choice and the concurrency utilities that replaced raw synchronized blocks.

cards.prompt: What is the generational hypothesis, and how do JVM collectors exploit it?
cards.answer: Most objects die young. Collectors therefore split the heap into a young generation collected often and cheaply, and an old generation collected rarely and expensively; survivors are promoted between them.
cards.explanation: Young collection is a copying collector over live objects only, so its cost scales with survivors, not with garbage. G1 (default) divides the heap into regions and targets a pause goal; ZGC and Shenandoah trade throughput for sub-millisecond pauses.

cards.prompt: You need a lookup by key, iteration in insertion order, and no duplicates. Which collection?
cards.answer: `LinkedHashMap` (or `LinkedHashSet` if the key is the whole value) — hash lookup plus a linked list maintaining insertion order.
cards.explanation: `HashMap` gives O(1) lookup and arbitrary order; `TreeMap` gives sorted order at O(log n); `LinkedHashMap` gives O(1) lookup with predictable iteration, and with `accessOrder=true` plus `removeEldestEntry` it becomes an LRU cache in ten lines.

cards.prompt: Why does this throw ConcurrentModificationException?
cards.answer: The for-each loop uses an iterator, and structurally modifying the list behind its back invalidates it. Use `list.removeIf(String::isEmpty)` or an explicit `Iterator` with `it.remove()`.
cards.explanation: Fail-fast iterators compare a modCount snapshot on every `next()`. The exception is a best-effort bug detector, not a guarantee — the same pattern across threads can silently corrupt instead. `removeIf` is both correct and clearer.

cards.prompt: `volatile` vs `synchronized`
cards.answer: volatile guarantees visibility and ordering for a single variable; synchronized additionally provides mutual exclusion over a block.

left.title: volatile
points: Right for a status flag or a published reference

right.title: synchronized
points: Right for invariants spanning several fields

cards.explanation: `count++` is read-modify-write: three operations. Volatile fixes visibility but not atomicity — use `AtomicInteger` or a lock. The Java Memory Model defines all of this in terms of happens-before edges, not in terms of caches.

cards.prompt: Why is `new Thread(...).start()` per request a bad idea in a server, and what replaces it?
cards.answer: Unbounded platform threads exhaust memory and thrash the scheduler. Use an `ExecutorService` with a bounded pool and a bounded queue — or virtual threads (Project Loom) for blocking I/O workloads.
cards.explanation: A platform thread costs ~1 MB of stack. A bounded pool applies backpressure instead of collapsing. Virtual threads (Java 21) are cheap enough to have one per request, which makes plain blocking code scale like async code. Before Java 24 (JEP 491) a virtual thread blocking inside `synchronized` pinned its carrier thread; on older JDKs prefer `ReentrantLock` in hot blocking paths.

cards.prompt: How many elements does `map` process here?
cards.code:
List.of(1,2,3,4,5).stream()
    .map(x -> { System.out.println("map " + x); return x * 2; })
    .filter(x -> x > 4)
    .findFirst();
cards.answer: Three — the pipeline is lazy and short-circuits at the first match (1→2 filtered, 2→4 filtered, 3→6 matches).
cards.explanation: Intermediate operations build a pipeline; only a terminal operation runs it, pulling elements one at a time. Short-circuiting terminals (`findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `limit`) stop early, so ordering your operations matters for cost.

modules.name: Modern Java Language
modules.description: Records, sealed types, pattern matching, Optional, generics wildcards, boxing and resource handling.

cards.prompt: What do sealed interfaces and pattern-matching `switch` give you together?
cards.answer: A sealed interface lists its permitted implementations (`sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square`), and a `switch` over it with record patterns (`case Circle(var r) -> ...`) is checked for exhaustiveness — no `default` needed, and adding a new permitted type breaks every incomplete switch at compile time.
cards.explanation: This is Java's version of algebraic data types, standard since Java 21. It replaces visitor-pattern boilerplate and `instanceof` chains for closed hierarchies such as ASTs, commands and results. Guards (`case Circle c when c.r() > 10 ->`) handle conditional cases.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer: true false true
cards.explanation: `Integer.valueOf` caches boxed values from -128 to 127, so autoboxed 127s are the same object and `==` is true; 128s are distinct objects. `==` on boxed types compares references — always use `.equals()`, or compare primitives. Unboxing a null `Integer` throws NullPointerException, another boxing trap.

cards.prompt: Three things here misuse `Optional`. What are they?
cards.answer: Optional as a field and as a parameter (it is designed as a return type only), and `isPresent()` + `get()`, which is a null check with extra steps. Return `Optional<Address>` from the lookup and use `map`, `orElse`, `orElseThrow` or `ifPresent` at the call site.
cards.explanation: Optional exists to make "may be absent" explicit in method signatures. It is not serialisable, adds an allocation, and a null Optional reference defeats the purpose. Never return `null` from a method declared to return Optional.

cards.prompt: What changed with switch expressions and text blocks?
cards.answer: Switch can now be an expression with arrow labels — `int days = switch (m) { case FEB -> 28; case APR, JUN, SEP, NOV -> 30; default -> 31; };` — with no fall-through and exhaustiveness checks for enums. Text blocks (`"""`) write multi-line strings without escapes.
cards.explanation: Arrow cases remove the classic missing-`break` bug. Use `yield` to return a value from a block case. Combined with `var` for local type inference, records and pattern matching, modern Java reads very differently from Java 8.

cards.prompt: What does PECS mean for `? extends T` and `? super T`?
cards.answer: "Producer extends, consumer super." Use `List<? extends Number>` when you only read `Number`s out of it (it produces them), and `List<? super Integer>` when you only write `Integer`s into it (it consumes them).
cards.explanation: Generics are invariant: a `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`, because you could then add a `Double` to it. Wildcards restore flexibility safely — this is exactly why `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` is declared that way.

cards.prompt: `Comparable` vs `Comparator`
cards.answer: `Comparable` defines a class's natural ordering inside the class (`compareTo`); `Comparator` is an external, pluggable ordering you can define many of.

right.title: Comparator<T>
points: Sorts classes you do not own

cards.explanation: Build comparators declaratively: `Comparator.comparing(Person::lastName).thenComparing(Person::age).reversed()`. Never compare with subtraction (`a - b`) — it overflows for large values; use `Integer.compare`. Keep `compareTo` consistent with `equals`, or sorted sets and maps will behave strangely.

cards.prompt: What does try-with-resources guarantee?
cards.answer: Every resource declared in `try (var in = ...; var out = ...)` that implements `AutoCloseable` is closed automatically, in reverse order, whether the block completes or throws. An exception from `close()` is attached as a suppressed exception rather than masking the original.
cards.explanation: It replaces error-prone `finally { if (x != null) x.close(); }` blocks, which lose the original exception when close also throws. It is Java's equivalent of Python's `with` and C#'s `using`.

cards.prompt: What can a Java enum do beyond naming constants?
cards.answer: Enums are full classes: constants can have fields, constructors, methods and even per-constant method bodies. `EnumMap` and `EnumSet` are compact, fast collections keyed by enum values, and enums are the simplest correct singleton.
cards.explanation: Switching on an enum is exhaustiveness-checked in switch expressions. Never persist `ordinal()` — reordering the constants silently corrupts stored data; persist `name()` or an explicit code field instead.

cards.prompt: Static nested class vs inner (non-static) class
cards.answer: A static nested class is just a class scoped inside another; an inner class holds a hidden reference to an instance of its enclosing class.

left.title: static nested
points: No reference to an outer instance

right.title: inner
points: Needs an outer instance to exist
Keeps the outer object alive — leak risk

cards.explanation: Default to `static` nested classes. An inner class — including anonymous classes — silently keeps its outer instance alive, which is a classic memory leak when the inner object (a listener, a task) outlives the outer one. Lambdas capture `this` only if they use it.

modules.name: JVM, Concurrency Utilities & Build
modules.description: The JVM and JIT, heap tuning, CompletableFuture, concurrent collections, Maven/Gradle and testing.

cards.prompt: What happens between `javac` and your code running fast?
cards.answer: `javac` compiles to platform-neutral bytecode in `.class` files. The JVM loads classes lazily, verifies the bytecode, interprets it, and the JIT compilers (C1, then C2) compile hot methods to optimised native code using runtime profiling.
cards.explanation: That is why Java services warm up and why benchmarks need JMH rather than a stopwatch. The JDK contains the compiler and tools; the JVM is the runtime. For fast startup — CLIs, serverless — GraalVM native image compiles ahead of time, and CDS/AOT caches shorten warm-up.

cards.prompt: A Java service dies with `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` after a few days. How do you investigate?
cards.answer: Run with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`, then open the dump in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM and look at the dominator tree for what retains the most memory. Rising old-gen usage after each full GC means a leak; a flat baseline with spikes means undersized heap or huge requests.
cards.explanation: In containers set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` rather than a fixed `-Xmx`, so the heap tracks the container limit and leaves room for metaspace, threads and direct buffers. Usual culprits: unbounded caches, static collections, ThreadLocals on pooled threads, and listeners never removed.

cards.prompt: What is `CompletableFuture`, and what are its sharp edges?
cards.answer: A composable future: chain with `thenApply`/`thenCompose`, combine with `thenCombine` and `allOf`, and handle failures with `exceptionally`/`handle`. It enables non-blocking pipelines without callbacks nested inside callbacks.
cards.explanation: Sharp edges: async methods without an executor run on the shared `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, so blocking I/O there starves everything else — pass a dedicated executor. Exceptions arrive wrapped in `CompletionException`, and `get()` without a timeout can block forever. With virtual threads, plain blocking code is often simpler.

cards.prompt: Several threads update a shared `HashMap` of counters and counts go missing. What do you use instead?
cards.answer: `ConcurrentHashMap` with atomic compound operations: `counts.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` or `compute`. Wrapping a HashMap in `Collections.synchronizedMap` works too but serialises every access.
cards.explanation: The trap is check-then-act: `if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, v)` is still racy on a concurrent map — use `putIfAbsent` or `computeIfAbsent`. For hot counters use `LongAdder`, which stripes updates across cells to avoid contention.

cards.prompt: Maven vs Gradle
cards.answer: Maven is declarative XML with a fixed lifecycle and strong conventions; Gradle is a programmable build (Kotlin or Groovy DSL) with incremental builds and a build cache.

right.title: Gradle
points: Incremental builds and a build cache
Flexible — and easy to make complex
Default for Android and Kotlin projects

cards.explanation: Both use the same repository and coordinate system (`group:artifact:version`), and both should be run through their wrapper scripts (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) so everyone uses the same build tool version. Pin dependency versions and use a BOM to keep library families aligned.

cards.prompt: What do JUnit 5, AssertJ and Mockito each contribute to a Java test suite?
cards.answer: JUnit 5 is the test runner and lifecycle (`@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@Nested`). AssertJ gives fluent, readable assertions (`assertThat(list).containsExactly(...)`). Mockito creates test doubles (`mock`, `when(...).thenReturn`, `verify`).
cards.explanation: Use Testcontainers for integration tests against a real database or broker in Docker instead of mocking the persistence layer. Mock only what you own or what is slow and external; over-mocking produces the brittle tests that break on every refactor.

cards.prompt: Cost of building a string of n parts with `s += part` in a loop versus a `StringBuilder`?
cards.answer: `+=` in a loop is O(n²) character copying because `String` is immutable and each concatenation creates a new string; `StringBuilder.append` is amortised O(1) per append, O(n) total.
cards.explanation: The compiler optimises concatenation within a single expression, but not across loop iterations. Use `StringBuilder` in loops, or `String.join` / `Collectors.joining` for collections. Same lesson as Python's `str.join`.
